papers.summary: Carbohydrate binding proteins (CBPs) are alluring and challenging targets in biology. CBPs achieve high-affinity interactions with their substrates through multivalent interactions with carbohydrates, often in branched, heterogeneous structures. Many cell recognition events and host-pathogen interactions are mediated by these carbohydrate-protein interactions. Therefore, the development of glycan-based mimics and disruptors of these interactions have applications in studying target CBPs, carbohydrate-based vaccines, immunomodulating agents, diagnostics, and therapeutics against cancer and other diseases. papers.summary: This article explores the dynamics of collaborative and participatory innovations in public health services using Chen et al.’s (2020) typology. Based on a mixed survey of projects awarded under the national “Droits des usagers de la santé” initiative, the study finds that user participation primarily generates operational and capacity-oriented innovations frequently involving external partnerships. papers.summary: This dissertation examines the Jewish Question in the Imperial Russian Press. It uses a dataset of 100 digitally available newspapers and journals to quantitatively and qualitatively analyze how frequently and in what context the Imperial Russian press mentioned Jewish people, and how that discourse changed over time and across genres. It addresses several key themes: the relationship between Russia’s Jewish and Christian populations, the effects of state and public discourse on Jews, and how all of this broadens our perspective on the “Jewish Question” in Imperial Russia.

papers.summary: Despite local successes, the circular economy has not yet succeeded in significantly reducing the consumption of virgin raw materials or environmental impacts on a global scale. Among many other causes, the notion of the circular economy rebound effect has recently been introduced to account for this shortcoming, although it remains relatively underexplored. This leads to two questions: “How do rebound effects manifest themselves in the circular economy?” and “How can these rebound effects be mitigated to achieve strong sustainability?” Drawing on a metanarrative literature review, this article provides an up-to-date synthesis of theoretical contributions to better understand the phenomenon of circular economy rebound effects. By cross-referencing critical studies on the circular economy, work advocating various forms of innovation and principles aligned with strong sustainability, the article also suggests five practical avenues to mitigate them across several systemic levels.
